question.text: Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are two events such that $P(A \cap B)=\dfrac{3}{8}$ and $P(B)=\dfrac{3}{4}.$ What is $P(A|B)?$
question.explanation:
We use the definition of the conditional probability $P(A|B){:}$

\[ P(A|B) = \dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)} \]

Substituting the given values, we get

\[ \eqalign{P(A|B) &= \dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\left(\dfrac38\right)}{\left(\dfrac34\right)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}. } \]

question.text: Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are two events such that $P(A \cap B)=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $P(A)=\dfrac{2}{3}.$ Find $P(B|A).$
question.explanation:
We use the definition of the conditional probability $P(B|A){:}$

\[ P(B|A) = \dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)} \]

Substituting the given values, we get

\begin{align*} P(B|A) &= \dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{4}. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Computing a Conditional Probability: Word Problems

question.text: In a group of kids, the probability that a kid likes oranges is $0.6,$ the probability that a kid likes oranges and apples is $0.3.$ If a kid who likes oranges is selected at random, what is the probability that the kid also likes apples?
question.explanation:
Let us call $O$ the event "the kid likes oranges" and $A$ the event "the kid likes apples."

The required probability is $P(A| O),$ which is given by

\[ P(A| O)= \dfrac{P(A\cap O)}{P(O)}. \]

We are given that \begin{align*} P(O) &=0.6,\\[3pt] P(A\cap O) &= 0.3. \end{align*}

Therefore, substituting the above into our formula for $P(A| O),$ we get \begin{align*} P(A |O) &= \dfrac{0.3}{0.6}= 0.5. \end{align*}

example.title: Computing a Conditional Probability: Word Problems

question.text: Two dice are thrown. Both dice land on the same number. What is the probability that this number is $5?$
question.explanation:
Let us call $F$ the event "both dice landed on $5$" and $E$ the event "both dice landed on the same number."

The required probability is $P(F | E)$, which is given by

\[ P(F|E) = \dfrac{P(F\cap E)}{P(E)}. \]

Let's find $P(E)$ and $P(F \cap E).$

  • There are $6$ possibilities of getting the same number on both dice among the $6\times 6=36$ possible combinations. So, we have \[ P(E) = \dfrac{6}{36} = \dfrac16 . \]

  • There is only one possibility to get $5$ on both dice. So, we have \[ P(F\cap E) = \dfrac{1}{36}. \]

Therefore, substituting the above into our formula for $P(F|E),$ we get \[ P(F|E) = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{1}{36}\right)}{\left(\dfrac16\right)} = \dfrac{1}{6}. \]

exampleAnswers.title: Computing a Probability Using the Multiplication Law for Conditional Probability

question.text: Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are two events such that $P(A|B)=0.6,$ $P(A)=0.6,$ $P(B)=0.8.$ Find $P(B|A).$
question.explanation:
Use the multiplication law, we have

\begin{align} P(A\cap B) &= P(B) \cdot P(A|B) \\[5pt] &= 0.8 \cdot 0.6 \\[5pt] &= 0.48. \end{align}

To compute $P(B|A),$ we use

\[ P(B|A) = \dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)}. \]

Substituting the known values into the above, we get

\begin{align*} P(B|A) &= \dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{0.48}{0.6} \\[5pt] &= 0.8. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Computing a Probability Using the Multiplication Law for Conditional Probability: Word Problems

question.text: Two cards are randomly drawn from a pack of $52$ cards one by one without replacement. What is the probability that both the cards are diamonds?
question.explanation:
Let us call $D_1$ the event "the first card drawn is a diamond" and $D_2$ the event "the second card drawn is a diamond."

The required probability is $P(D_1\cap D_2),$ which is given by

\[ P(D_1\cap D_2) = P(D_1) \cdot P(D_2|D_1). \]

Let's find $P(D_1)$ and $P(D_2|D_1).$

  • There are $13$ diamonds among the $52$ cards, so we have \[ P(D_1) = \dfrac{13}{52}=\dfrac{1}{4}. \]

  • If the first card drawn is a diamond, there are $12$ diamonds left in the pack among the remaining $51$ cards. So, we have \[ P(D_2|D_1) = \dfrac{12}{51}. \]

Substituting the above data into the multiplication law for conditional probability, we get

\[ P(D_1\cap D_2)=\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{12}{51}=\dfrac{1}{17}. \]

example.title: Computing a Probability Using the Multiplication Law for Conditional Probability: Word Problems

question.text:
An orange bag and a black bag contain various items. The orange bag contains five balls labeled $5,$ $7,$ $8,$ $8,$ and $10.$ The black bag contains four balls labeled $M,$ $ M,$ $N, $ and $O.$

A bag is chosen at random, and a single item is picked at random from the chosen bag. What is the probability that a ball labeled $N$ is drawn?
question.explanation:
Let us call $B$ the event "the black bag is chosen" and $N$ the event "a ball labeled $N$ is drawn."

The required probability is $P(B\cap N),$ which is given by

\[ P(B\cap N) = P(B) \cdot P(N|B). \]

Let's find $P(B)$ and $P(N|B).$

  • There is $1$ black bag among the $2$ bags, so we have \[ P(B) = \dfrac12. \]

  • There is $1$ ball labeled $N$ among the $4$ items in the black bag. So, we have \[ P(N|B) = \dfrac14. \]

Substituting the above data into the multiplication law for conditional probability, we get

\[ P(B\cap N)=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac14=\dfrac18. \]
